newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 29.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 29.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents.
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- RIVAL BANK'S ROAD RAGE OVER F1 FLOAT

Investment bank Goldman Sachs has been forced off the track by rivals Salomon Brothers in a row over whether Goldman was trying to muscle in on the floatation of motor racing group Formula One. Salomon moved to exclude Goldman from the syndicate of 16 banks handling the float following news of a meeting last week between John Thornton, managing director of Goldman Sachs, and Bernie Eccleston of Formula One Holdings.
-- ANDERSEN 23 MILLION STG BILL FOR HITCHES TO NI COMPUTER
Management consultants Andersen Consulting has paid a 23 million stg bill to cover costs involved in a troubled government computer contract. Andersen was awarded the contract

-- to computerise 64 million National Insurance records -- in 1995 after cutting its tender by 100 million stg to 45 million stg. After paying 3.1 million stg to the National Audit Office following late delivery of the project, Andersen says it will also lose 8 million stg revenues and face extra costs of 8.5 million stg.
-- WATER GROUPS MAY PAY LESS WINDFALL TAX

Research carried out by SBC Warburg has found that water companies will escape the worst of a possible 5 billion stg windfall profits tax should the Treasury decide to use turnover as the basis for the levy. However, should turnover be chosen as the criteria, regional electricity companies will face much steeper bills, the bank said.
THE TIMES
-- ANGLIAN SAYS WINDFALL TAX WILL DELAY PRICE CUTS

Anglian Water, one of the privatised utilities that threatened to challenge the government's planned windfall tax, has conceded that the levy is likely to be legal. However, the company warned Wednesday that the tax would mean less cash for investment and that customer price cuts will be delayed.
-- JOBS AND EMU GET EQUAL BILLING BY COOK

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook has signalled the government's intention to support new European Union employment provisions, but stressed that the initiatives should have equal weight with meeting the financial criteria of European monetary union.
However, the indication of support for the employment initiatives prompted British business leaders to say they would oppose the move.
-- BATTLE CALLS EMERGENCY ELECTRICITY MEETING

Energy minister John Battle is to call an emergency summit of the heads of all of Britain's regional electricity companies following a meeting with industry regulator Professor Stephen Littlechild. The summit comes amid speculation the government could be forced to delay the introduction of competition in the domestic electricity market. However, Battle stressed his desire to see competition introduced on schedule, saying, "we cannot afford a crisis of confidence in energy markets at this stage".
THE GUARDIAN
-- BUILDING SOCIETIES TAKE TAX DISPUTE TO EUROPE

The British government has been challenged in the European Court of Human Rights by three UK building societies over the issue of tax payments totalling more than 80 million stg. The case has been brought by the National & Provincial, Leeds Permanent and the Yorkshire building society, who claim they suffered double taxation when the Conservative government changed the way it collected income tax on the interest paid to customers with savings accounts.
-- THORN ADMITS THE PAINFUL TRUTH

Rental group Thorn has offered shareholders 87 million stg in a hand-out that has been seen as an attempted apology for the company's poor performance since its demerger from EMI last year. Shares in the company had been 408p at the time of the demerger last August. On Wednesday, they closed at 155.5p. The underlying reason for the decline is the company's failure of plans to expand its TV and video rental business.
-- COMPASS TURNS TO WEST FOR COLLEGE CATERER

Fast-growing British group Compass is to acquire Daka International, an American caterer specialising in schools, for $195 million (119.8 million stg). Compass recently became the world's largest contract caterer, and earlier this month became caterer for London's Wembley and Oval stadia with another acquisition. The Daka deal will enable the company to "build on its position as a leading food service provider in the US education market", said Compass chief executive USA Mike Bailey.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- CHANCELLOR SELECTS BANK COMMITTEE

Chancellor Gordon Brown has appointed three highly respected academics to the Bank of England's new Monetary Policy Committee, leaving just one of the four outside appointments left to fill. The three will reassure sceptics in the financial markets who feared that Brown would make politically motivated appointments. The three men, all monetary policy experts, are David Currie of the LSE, John Fleming of Wadham College, Oxford, and Charles Goodhart, a professor of finance at the LSE.
-- SIR JOHN EGAN CLAIMS HOTEL PRICES THREATEN TOURIST TRADE

Sir John Egan, chairman of the London Tourist Board, has warned that inflation-busting price increases over the past three years by London hoteliers could lead to the loss of business to other European cities. The comments, made in a private letter to hoteliers, follows research by the LTB that found tour operators were reporting that London had dropped from first to third place in Europe's most popular city destinations.
-- CELLTECH PROFITS DELAY

Celltech, the drug development company, has said it does not now expect to be profitable until 2000, two years later than anticipated, following the failure of its lead drug for septic shock. Announcing results for the six months to March 31, Celltech chief executive Peter Fellner said the group's followup treatment for the bowel condition "Crohn's disease" would replace at least a third of the value the company lost last week after being forced to abandon trials of the sepsis drug.
